steps.text:
I'm trying to figure out whether this netsh firewall rule naming "python.exe" is benign — it resembles what Windows normally adds when a user allows an app through the Defender Firewall prompt, like with Python's http.server, though that's usually triggered by the firewall UI rather than netsh run from PowerShell.

Given it's the OTRF simulation dataset for Python HTTP server usage, and the script opens both TCP/UDP rules from PowerShell while serving the full user profile directory to any remote IP, this looks like deliberate exposure of user data rather than a normal firewall prompt — I'm leaning malicious, with the firewall rule changes needing cleanup verification.

I'm flagging this as malicious based on behavior alone — no attacker connections or payload were found, but within two seconds a PowerShell session opened the firewall network-wide and launched a web server exposing the entire user profile folder.

At 04:16:10.218 it ran a second netsh (proc-e83ff48032) to add the same rule for UDP. Both rules were named 'python.exe' with description 'python.exe', which copies the name Windows gives rules it creates automatically. At 04:16:10.367 it started python.exe (proc-f532449bf1) from C:\\Users\\wardog\\AppData\\Local\\Programs\\Python\\Python39 with '-m http.server 8000', working directory C:\\Users\\wardog\\. That serves the whole user profile to any host on the network. PowerShell also opened python.exe with full access (0x1fffff). The scripted firewall bypass, the look-alike rule names and the open share of the profile folder fit staging data for exfiltration or tool transfer. No connections to the server were seen. Scripted firewall bypass plus an open share of the profile fits data staging or exfiltration. No connections to the server were seen.
